intro_text.en: Unit 5 of Mechanical Drafting (DI02000121) brings the subject's drawing skills together: the assembly drawing of a 4-5 part mechanism, orthographic projections of each component, the fundamentals of the detail (part) drawing, the Bill of Materials (BOM) that ties the two together, and reading of industrial assembly examples. Practicals 5 and 6 - assembly drawing with BOM, and detail drawing - are the direct application of this unit.

title.en: 5.1-5.2 Assembly drawings, detail drawings and the BOM
title.gu: 5.1-5.2 Assembly drawings, detail drawings and the BOM

h.en: 5.1 Concept of assembly drawing (4-5 mechanical parts)
h.gu: 5.1 Concept of assembly drawing (4-5 mechanical parts)

body.en:
What an assembly drawing is for

An assembly drawing shows the components of a product in their working relationship - assembled, usually in one or two views (very often sectioned) - so that the fitter knows what goes where, in which orientation, and how it is fastened. It is the drawing of the product, not of any single part: it answers 'how does it fit together and does it work?', while sizes of individual parts live on the detail drawings (Card 5.2).

Rules of the assembly view

  • Show the minimum views that explain assembly - a sectional front view plus one end view is typical; section through the main axis to expose internal parts.
  • Adjacent parts are hatched in different directions/spacings (Unit 2); the same part keeps one pattern everywhere. Shafts, bolts, nuts, studs, screws, rivets and keys are not section-lined.
  • Each part is identified by a balloon (circle with the part number, Leader to the part) keyed to the parts list - see the flange coupling in the diagram: flanges 1-2, bolts 3, nuts 4, shafts 5-6.
  • Only assembly dimensions are given: overall size, centre distances, mounting dimensions and the fits between mating parts written as fit designations (dia. 50 H7/g6). Part-manufacturing dimensions are deliberately NOT repeated (they would risk contradiction with the detail drawings).

Component projections

Before assembling on paper, every component must exist as orthographic projections (from its detail drawing or a preceding exercise): the assembly exercise of this unit (4-5 parts) starts by projecting each part - flange: disc with hub and bolt holes; shaft: stepped cylinder with keyway; key; standard bolt/nut - checking that mating surfaces share diameters and datums, then composing them in working position.

h.en: 5.2 Fundamentals of detail drawing, BOM and assembly drawing
h.gu: 5.2 Fundamentals of detail drawing, BOM and assembly drawing

body.en:
The detail (part) drawing

A detail drawing completely defines ONE component for manufacture: sufficient views (with sections where needed), every dimension with its limits or fit designation, surface-texture symbols, GD&T where function requires, material, heat treatment, general notes and a filled title block. Test of completeness: a machinist with no other document can make the part and an inspector can accept it. The flange detail in the diagram shows the pattern: sectional view carrying diameters and the bore fit, end view locating the 4-hole pattern on its PCD, finish symbol on the seating face, nothing left to guess.

The Bill of Materials (BOM)

The BOM / parts list (diagram md5_bom) is the table married to the assembly drawing: columns for part (balloon) number, part name, material, quantity per assembly, and remarks/standard specification. Manufactured parts point to their detail drawings; standard parts (bolts, nuts, bearings, keys to IS/ISO specs) are bought out - they are listed with their standard designation and are never drawn in detail. The BOM drives purchasing, stores, costing and spare-parts supply - an error here stops production as surely as a wrong dimension.

Assembly drawing vs detail drawing (keep them straight)

AspectAssembly drawingDetail drawing
Purposehow parts fit & work togetherhow one part is made
Dimensionsoverall, mounting, fits onlyevery manufacturing size + tolerances
Identificationballoons + BOMtitle block, material, finish, GD&T
Used byfitter/assembler, purchaser (via BOM)machinist, inspector

h.en: 5.3 Industrial example assemblies - how to read them
h.gu: 5.3 Industrial example assemblies - how to read them

body.en:
The reading method (applies to any industrial assembly)

Take the two standard teaching examples of this course - the bench vice and the plummer block (equally: flange coupling of the diagram, tool post, screw jack):

  • Step 1 - title and BOM first: name the product, count the parts, note materials and which items are standard (vice: body, sliding jaw, screw, handle bar, jaw plates, nuts/pins; plummer block: pedestal, cap, brasses/bearing halves, bolts).
  • Step 2 - find the working principle: follow the power/motion path: vice handle -> screw (rotates in the fixed nut in the body) -> sliding jaw advances; plummer block: shaft rotates in the split bearing, cap bolts clamp the brasses with a controlled clearance.
  • Step 3 - read each interface: which pair slides (jaw in body guide - clearance fit), which is fixed (screw collar, bearing cap), which fastener locks it - and confirm each has a balloon, a fit and a detail drawing.
  • Step 4 - imagine the assembly sequence: what is placed first, what cannot be inserted later (a classic trap: a part trapped by a later one), and how it is dismantled for maintenance.

What industry expects from this exercise

A diploma engineer reads an assembly to prepare process plans, BOMs for purchasing, and erection/maintenance instructions (the rationale of this course). Practising the four steps on 1-2 real assemblies converts drawing knowledge into the reading fluency the job demands - and Practicals 5-6 then make you produce the same documents.

h.en: Practical 5: Draw assembly drawing with Bill of Materials (BOM)
h.gu: Practical 5: Draw assembly drawing with Bill of Materials (BOM)

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 5)

Prepare the assembly drawing of a 4-5 part mechanism with balloons and a complete Bill of Materials.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Obtain/project the orthographic views of each component; verify mating diameters and centre distances agree.
  • Step 2: Compose the assembly in working position; choose the section through the main axis; hatch adjacent parts differently; leave shafts/fasteners unsectioned.
  • Step 3: Add balloons with leaders to every part, assembly dimensions and mating fit designations.
  • Step 4: Fill the BOM: part numbers matching balloons, names, materials, quantities, standard specifications for bought-out parts.

Result (report format)

Submit the A2 assembly sheet with BOM. Conclusion: describe the function of the assembly and the role/fit of each numbered part in one line each.

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 6)

Prepare a manufacturing-complete detail drawing of an assigned component (taken from the Practical 5 assembly).

Procedure

  • Step 1: Choose views (plus section) that describe the part with minimum views; fix datums consistent with the assembly interfaces.
  • Step 2: Dimension completely - every size once, from functional datums, with limit/fit designations on mating sizes.
  • Step 3: Add surface-texture symbols, GD&T frames where required, material, general tolerance note and title block.
  • Step 4: Completeness audit: could a machinist make it and an inspector check it without asking anything?

Result (report format)

Submit the A2 detail sheet. Conclusion: list the manufacturing operations the part needs (turning, drilling, milling...) in sequence, as read from your own drawing.

h.en: Q1. What is an assembly drawing? State its purpose and four conventions used in it.
h.gu: Q1. What is an assembly drawing? State its purpose and four conventions used in it.

body.en:
Model answer

An assembly drawing shows the parts of a product in their assembled, working relationship, so the fitter can assemble, and others can understand, service and order spares for the product. Conventions: (1) parts are identified by balloon numbers with leaders, keyed to the parts list/BOM; (2) adjacent parts are section-lined in different directions or spacings, while shafts, bolts, nuts, studs, screws and keys are shown unsectioned; (3) only assembly dimensions are given - overall, mounting and centre dimensions and mating fits (e.g. dia. 50 H7/g6) - part-manufacturing dimensions are not repeated; (4) minimum views, usually including a section through the principal axis, are used. (Diagram md5_assembly illustrates all four.)

Model answer

h.en: Q2. What is a detail drawing? What must it contain to be manufacturing-complete?
h.gu: Q2. What is a detail drawing? What must it contain to be manufacturing-complete?

body.en:
Model answer

A detail drawing completely defines a single component for manufacture. It must contain: enough orthographic views with sections to describe the shape unambiguously; every dimension, once only, dimensioned from functional datums, with limits/fit designations on mating sizes; surface-texture symbols on functional surfaces; GD&T feature control frames where form/position is functionally critical; material specification and any heat treatment or process notes; and a complete title block (name, number, scale, material, general tolerances). The test: a machinist can make the part and an inspector accept it from this sheet alone.

h.en: Q3. What is a Bill of Materials? Draw its format and state the information in each column.
h.gu: Q3. What is a Bill of Materials? Draw its format and state the information in each column.

body.en:
Model answer

The Bill of Materials (parts list) is the table accompanying an assembly drawing that lists every component of the assembly. Standard columns (as in md5_bom): Part No. - the balloon number used on the drawing; Part Name - e.g. 'Flange (left)'; Material - CI, EN8, MS...; Quantity - number required per assembly; Remarks - drawing number for manufactured parts or the standard specification (e.g. Hex bolt M12x90, IS 1363) for bought-out standard parts. The BOM links drawing, purchasing, stores and costing.

h.en: Q4. Differentiate between assembly drawing and detail drawing (any four points).
h.gu: Q4. Differentiate between assembly drawing and detail drawing (any four points).

body.en:
Model answer

(1) Purpose: assembly drawing shows how parts fit and work together; detail drawing shows how one part is made. (2) Dimensions: assembly carries only overall, mounting and fit dimensions; detail carries every manufacturing dimension with tolerances. (3) Identification: assembly identifies parts by balloons and a BOM; detail uses its title block with material, finish and GD&T. (4) Users: fitters, purchasers and maintenance use the assembly; machinists and inspectors use the detail. (5) Views: assembly usually shows parts joined, often in one sectioned view; detail shows the isolated part in as many views as its shape needs. (Any four.)

h.en: Q5. Why are standard parts like bolts and nuts not drawn in detail in an assembly?
h.gu: Q5. Why are standard parts like bolts and nuts not drawn in detail in an assembly?

body.en:
Model answer

Standard parts are bought ready-made to national/international standards, so manufacturing information for them is unnecessary and would only duplicate the standard. On the assembly they are shown in position by simplified conventional shapes, identified by balloons, and fully specified in the BOM by their standard designation - e.g. 'Hex bolt M12 x 90 - IS 1363' - which tells purchasing exactly what to buy. Only their presence, fit and tightening matter to the assembly.

h.en: Q6. State the rules for sectioning parts in an assembly drawing.
h.gu: Q6. State the rules for sectioning parts in an assembly drawing.

body.en:
Model answer

(1) Adjacent parts are hatched at different angles or spacings so each part reads as a separate piece; the same part keeps the identical pattern in all views. (2) Parts whose section adds nothing - solid shafts, bolts, nuts, studs, screws, rivets, keys, pins - are conventionally not section-lined when the plane passes along their axis. (3) Thin parts like gaskets may be blackened solid. (4) Hatching stops at part boundaries; no hatch line may cross into a neighbouring part. (5) Hidden lines are minimised, being replaced by the section itself.

(3) Thin parts like gaskets may be blackened solid. (4) Hatching stops at part boundaries; no hatch line may cross into a neighbouring part. (5) Hidden lines are minimised, being replaced by the section itself.

h.en: Q7. How will you read an industrial assembly drawing systematically?
h.gu: Q7. How will you read an industrial assembly drawing systematically?

body.en:
Model answer

Four steps: (1) title block and BOM - identify the product, count parts, separate manufactured from standard parts; (2) trace the working principle - follow the path of motion/power through the mechanism (e.g. vice handle to screw to sliding jaw); (3) study interfaces - which surfaces slide, locate or fix, their fits and fasteners, checking balloon, fit and detail-drawing references agree; (4) plan the assembly sequence mentally - order of fitting, access for tools, and how it can be dismantled. This routine turns a dense industrial sheet into a working understanding for process planning and maintenance.

h.en: Q8. What are balloon numbers? Where is the balloon placed and what does it connect?
h.gu: Q8. What are balloon numbers? Where is the balloon placed and what does it connect?

body.en:
Model answer

A balloon is a small circle containing the part number of a component, placed outside the view near the part, with a Leader line ending in an arrow (or dot) on the part itself. Balloons are arranged in an orderly row/column without crossing leaders, numbered in a logical order (size or assembly sequence). The balloon number is the key that connects the picture of the part on the assembly drawing to its row in the Bill of Materials and, for manufactured parts, to its detail drawing number.

body.en:
ASSEMBLY: fit-together + balloons + BOM + assembly dimensions only. DETAIL: one part + all sizes/limits + finish + GD&T + material.

Manufacturing reads details; assembly reads the product. Dimensions live on details - never duplicated on the assembly.

  • Step 4: Fill the BOM: part numbers matching balloons, names, materials, quantities, standard specifications for bought-out parts.

Result (report format)

Submit the A2 assembly sheet with BOM. Conclusion: describe the function of the assembly and the role/fit of each numbered part in one line each.
body.gu:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 5)

Prepare the assembly drawing of a 4-5 part mechanism with balloons and a complete Bill of Materials.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Obtain/project the orthographic views of each component; verify mating diameters and centre distances agree.
  • Step 2: Compose the assembly in working position; choose the section through the main axis; hatch adjacent parts differently; leave shafts/fasteners unsectioned.
  • Step 3: Add balloons with leaders to every part, assembly dimensions and mating fit designations.
  • Step 4: Fill the BOM: part numbers matching balloons, names, materials, quantities, standard specifications for bought-out parts.

Result (report format)

Submit the A2 assembly sheet with BOM. Conclusion: describe the function of the assembly and the role/fit of each numbered part in one line each.

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 6)

Prepare a manufacturing-complete detail drawing of an assigned component (taken from the Practical 5 assembly).

Procedure

  • Step 1: Choose views (plus section) that describe the part with minimum views; fix datums consistent with the assembly interfaces.
  • Step 2: Dimension completely - every size once, from functional datums, with limit/fit designations on mating sizes.
  • Step 3: Add surface-texture symbols, GD&T frames where required, material, general tolerance note and title block.
  • Step 4: Completeness audit: could a machinist make it and an inspector check it without asking anything?

Result (report format)

Submit the A2 detail sheet. Conclusion: list the manufacturing operations the part needs (turning, drilling, milling...) in sequence, as read from your own drawing.
